code:
some_long_command

# Runs in the foreground; your prompt disappears and waits until the command finishes

Ctrl+C

# Sends an interrupt signal to the foreground process; politely asks it to stop immediately

some_server &

# The & at the end runs the command in the background; your prompt returns immediately

# The shell prints the background job's PID (process ID number) so you can track it

ps aux | grep ollama

# ps aux lists every running process on the system with details

# grep ollama filters to only lines mentioning "ollama"; shows PID, CPU, memory

kill 12345

# Sends a polite termination signal (SIGTERM) to process number 12345

# Replace 12345 with the actual PID from ps aux

kill -9 12345

# Sends an immediate, uncatchable kill signal (SIGKILL); use only if kill 12345 fails

# The process cannot clean up after itself, so use this as a last resort
description: Walk through stopping foreground commands, starting background servers with &, finding process IDs with ps and grep, and stopping processes with kill.

steps.description: A normal command runs in the foreground and holds your prompt until it finishes. Pressing `Ctrl+C` sends an interrupt signal (`SIGINT`) that asks the foreground process to stop immediately.
Adding `&` at the end of `some_server &` starts the process in the background, prints its numeric Process ID (PID), and gives your shell prompt right back.
`ps aux | grep ollama` lists every running process on the machine and filters for lines mentioning `ollama` so you can find its PID, CPU usage, and memory usage.

`kill 12345` sends a polite termination signal (`SIGTERM`) so PID `12345` can clean up and exit. If the process is frozen and ignores `kill`, `kill -9 12345` sends `SIGKILL` to force the operating system to stop it immediately.

title: Managing foreground and background processes
